title: Understanding high- and low-quality URL Sharing on COVID-19 Twitter streams
screen_reason: Measures the share of COVID-19 hashtag tweets, retweets and quotes that carry URLs from a list of 1,249 low-quality/misinformation domains, with explicit denominators (Table 2): 0.83% of original tweets, 0.19% of retweets, 0.3% of all 67.6M posts, and 2.7% of all posts containing a link. Denominator is shared items, so SHARING (content_share). A secondary source-level 'reliability' classification of news domains is kept as a borderline QUALITY row.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language hashtags; author-acknowledged US/English list bias)
estimates.measure_type: % of all COVID-19 hashtag posts (tweets + quotes + retweets) that contained a URL from a low-quality/misinformation domain list
estimates.value_raw: Table 2, Combined row: LQMS URL Count 199,334 (0.3%) of 67,602,036 posts
estimates.denominator: 67,602,036 posts (11,276,874 original tweets + 1,500,099 quotes + 54,825,063 retweets) collected via the Twitter Streaming API on 14 English COVID-19 hashtags, 16 January - 15 April 2020
estimates.definition: the post contained a URL whose web domain appeared on the aggregated list of 1,249 low-quality/misinformation sources (NewsGuard COVID misinformation list plus the 'fake' category of the Zimdars, MBFC, PolitiFact, DailyDot and Allcott et al. lists)
estimates.misinfo_def: "NewsGuard is a journalistic organization that generally rates websites on their tendency to spread true or false information. Since the COVID-19 outbreak, they have kept a separate list of websites identified as propagating misinformation specifically related to the virus." The paper's conceptual definition: "Health misinformation—often defined as information that counters best available evidence from medical experts at the time".
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Domain-level classification only, no content coding and therefore no inter-coder reliability. Low-quality list = union of NewsGuard's COVID-19 misinformation tracking list and the 'fake' subcategory of five scholar/fact-checker lists (Zimdars et al., Media Bias/Fact Check, PolitiFact, Daily Dot, Allcott et al.), 1,249 domains in total. The authors concede "Considering only the domain, rather than the content itself, is a relatively blunt measure of misinformation" and that high-quality sites occasionally share misinformation and vice versa. 92% of URL content resolved and downloaded.
estimates.moderator_quote: Using the Twitter Streaming API, we began collecting tweets related to COVID19 on January 16, 2020. Data collection continues, but the data we present in this study is from January 16, 2020 to April 15, 2020.
estimates.notes: Conversation-level denominator: every post in the COVID-19 hashtag corpus, including the ~89% that contain no link at all. This is the figure behind the abstract's claim that misinformation is 'a relatively small proportion of the overall conversation'. The companion row with the link-only denominator (2.7%) is the more comparable figure for a synthesis of link-sharing studies.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language hashtags; author-acknowledged US/English list bias)
estimates.measure_type: % of shared links in the COVID-19 Twitter corpus that pointed to a low-quality/misinformation domain
estimates.value_raw: "LQMS represent 2.7%" of links (TNS over 20%, HQHS 1.8%); consistent with Table 2's 199,334 LQMS of 7,275,642 URL-bearing posts
estimates.denominator: 7,275,642 posts containing a URL (10.8% of the 67,602,036 collected posts), 16 January - 15 April 2020
estimates.definition: the shared URL's web domain appeared on the aggregated list of 1,249 low-quality/misinformation sources
estimates.misinfo_def: "NewsGuard is a journalistic organization that generally rates websites on their tendency to spread true or false information. Since the COVID-19 outbreak, they have kept a separate list of websites identified as propagating misinformation specifically related to the virus."
estimates.source_quote: Here, links to TNS comprise over 20% of links in our dataset, while LQMS represent 2.7% and HQHS account for 1.8%.
estimates.page_loc: Findings, 'Sharing of high quality health, traditional news, and low-quality sources' (p. 352)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 1,249-domain low-quality list and domain-level procedure as the other rows; no content coding, no reliability statistics.
estimates.moderator_quote: Our analysis of tweets related to the disease shows that 40.04% of original tweet content, 4.85% of the retweeted content, and 10.76% of the overall content includes a URL.
estimates.notes: Same country x platform cell as the 0.3% row, with the denominator narrowed from all posts to posts carrying a link - hence definition_variant = true. This is the link-level share and is roughly 9x the conversation-level share, purely because most COVID-19 tweets contain no URL. Note the paper also says LQMS and HQHS together are 'less than 5% of the overall shared URL content', consistent with 2.7% + 1.8%.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language hashtags; author-acknowledged US/English list bias)
estimates.measure_type: % of ORIGINAL COVID-19 hashtag tweets that contained a URL from a low-quality/misinformation domain
estimates.value_raw: "low-quality/fake news sources (LQMS) account for 0.83% of original tweets"; Table 2 Original Tweets row: 93,894 (0.8%) of 11,276,874
estimates.denominator: 11,276,874 original tweets (non-retweet, non-quote) in the COVID-19 hashtag corpus, 16 January - 15 April 2020
estimates.definition: the original tweet contained a URL whose web domain appeared on the 1,249-domain low-quality/misinformation list
estimates.misinfo_def: "NewsGuard is a journalistic organization that generally rates websites on their tendency to spread true or false information. Since the COVID-19 outbreak, they have kept a separate list of websites identified as propagating misinformation specifically related to the virus."
estimates.source_quote: Finally, low-quality/fake news sources (LQMS) account for 0.83% of original tweets and 0.19% of retweets.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same 1,249-domain low-quality list; domain-level, no content coding, no reliability statistics.
estimates.moderator_quote: We begin by identifying all of the URLs that are shared in each tweet, retweet, and quote in our data set.
estimates.notes: Original-tweet subset of the same measure, entered because the paper reports it in the running text with two decimals and because the original-vs-retweet contrast is substantive: the same sentence gives 0.19% for retweets (Table 2: 104,680 of 54,825,063) and Table 2 gives 0.05% for quotes (760 of 1,500,099). Only the original-tweet figure is entered as a row; the retweet and quote figures are recorded here and in missed_or_uncertain to avoid four near-duplicate rows. Note original tweets are far likelier to contain any URL at all (40.0%) than retweets (4.8%), which is what drives the difference.

estimates.country: not stated (English-language hashtags; author-acknowledged US/English list bias)
estimates.date: webpages downloaded March and late April 2020 (URLs shared 16 January - 15 April 2020)
estimates.measure_type: % of frequently-shared traditional news domains classified 'no reliability', i.e. whose shared articles linked only to low-quality misinformation sources
estimates.value_raw: 66 (16.22%) of 407 news domains have no reliability; 272 (66.83%) high, 31 (7.62%) mixed, 38 (9.34%) low
estimates.denominator: 407 of the 478 traditional news domains mentioned in at least 100 tweets that contained at least one article linking to at least one high-quality health source or low-quality misinformation source
estimates.definition: the news domain's shared articles contained outbound links to low-quality misinformation domains only (0% high-quality references) - 'no reliability'; high reliability >=80% high-quality references, mixed 50-80%, low <50%
estimates.misinfo_def: "We say a news site has high reliability if it references high quality information sources at least 80% of the time... it has no reliability if it links to only low quality content."
estimates.source_quote: We evaluated this subset and found that 272 out of 407 (66.83%) of these sources have high reliability, 31 (7.62%) have mixed reliability, 38 (9.34%) have low reliability and 66 (16.22%) have no reliability.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Author-defined reliability tiers computed from the outbound hyperlink composition of each domain's shared webpages (share of links going to the 39 HQHS domains vs the 1,249 LQMS domains); no veracity judgement of any article. The authors caveat: "the reliability labels used here solely describe the reliability of content from those sources shared on Twitter" and "it is possible that some of these news sites are debunking the information posted on the LQMS".
estimates.moderator_quote: Focusing on more frequently shared news sources (news domains), we find that 478 news domains were mentioned in at least 100 tweets.
estimates.notes: JUDGEMENT CALL, flagged borderline and coded QUALITY (kept, excluded from prevalence). This is a share of WEBSITES labelled unreliable, which the schema's CONTENT definition nominally admits, but the label rests entirely on outbound-link composition rather than on any truth judgement: a wholly accurate news outlet is labelled 'no reliability' if the handful of its articles shared on Twitter happened to link to a misinformation site - including, as the authors themselves note, while debunking it. Per the rule that a label a wholly true item can receive is QUALITY, and that genuine ambiguity resolves to QUALITY + borderline. The denominator is also doubly truncated (>=100 tweets AND at least one HQHS/LQMS outbound link), hence denom_selection = curated. The long-tail counterpart (domains mentioned in <100 tweets) is 242 of 850 (28.47%) with no reliability, 567 (66.71%) high, 26 (3.06%) mixed, 15 (1.76%) low - not entered as a second row.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) Retweets (0.19%; Table 2: 104,680 of 54,825,063) and quotes (0.05%; 760 of 1,500,099) are verbatim and eligible but were folded into the original-tweet row's notes rather than entered as two more near-duplicate rows of the same measure. An adjudicator who wants item-type granularity can add them directly from Table 2. (2) LIST SENSITIVITY - highly relevant to this review but not entered as rows because it would require me to build shares from Table 3's raw counts. Table 3 gives combined LQMS tweet counts per blacklist: MBFC 149,132, NewsGuard 61,199, DAILYDOT 7,752, ALLCOTT 6,921, ZIMDARS 2,472, POLITIFACT 1,241 - a 120-fold range across ground-truth lists for the same corpus, and the authors state 'the prevalence of low quality content depends significantly on which list is chosen to make that judgement'. The union list (1,249 domains) yields the 199,334 figure entered above. Pairwise daily-volume correlations are 0.43-0.93 (Table 4). (3) High-quality health source shares (0.55% of tweets, 0.12% of retweets, 0.2% combined, 1.8% of links) and traditional news shares (7.6% / 1.2% / 2.2% / over 20%) are reliable-source shares, not misinformation - no rows. (4) 'over 110,390 [tweets] have links to webpages from low quality sources' among shared traditional-news webpages is a raw count with no clear denominator and the authors cannot say whether the links debunk or endorse - no row. (5) No CONCENTRATION row is codeable: the paper reports network Gini coefficients of node DEGREE (LQMS 0.6560, TNS 0.6516, HQHS 0.5219) and hub-and-spoke disassortativity, but never a top-X%-of-users/sources share of exposure or sharing, so R1's two required quantities are absent. (6) Figure 2 shows the daily proportion of the conversation made up by each source type (declining across the period) but is an image; no daily value is readable, and the entered estimates are already period-level. (7) The 'top 10 domains' table (Table 1) contains no misinformation domain and gives tweet/user frequencies only. (8) Several figures in the introduction and related work are cited from other papers (Kouzy et al. 33.8%; 700 of 1,000 antibiotics tweets containing misinformation; 88% of Google Fact Check claims posted on social media) - excluded by R8 as figures the paper cites from elsewhere. (9) Reported exposure/reach is absent throughout: the study has no view, impression or user-level data.

rob.design: Observational platform-data study. Frame: Twitter Streaming API collection on 14 English COVID-19 hashtags (Appendix Table 6), 16 January - 15 April 2020, yielding 11,276,874 original tweets, 1,500,099 quotes and 54,825,063 retweets; a documented API glitch made some hashtags unavailable 13-15 March 2020. URLs extracted from the JSON records, redirects resolved, referenced webpages downloaded (March and late April 2020); 92% of URL content resolved and analysed, the unresolved remainder mostly non-resolving bit.ly links and non-HTML file types. Classification is entirely domain-level with no human content coding and hence no inter-coder reliability: 39 author-assembled high-quality health domains, the Media Bias/Fact Check list of reliable news domains (1,198 observed), and 1,249 low-quality/misinformation domains built as the union of NewsGuard's COVID misinformation list and the 'fake' subcategory of five scholar/fact-checker lists. Robustness is addressed by comparing the six lists (Table 3) and their daily-volume correlations (Table 4). Author-acknowledged limitations: the domain proxy misclassifies occasional accurate content on bad domains and vice versa, the lists are heavily US- and English-based, and hashtag-based collection cannot capture all COVID-19 conversation and may shift over time. No sampling weights, no response rate (not a survey), no country stratification.
rob.item6_quote: Low-quality/Misinformation Sources (LQMS) We identify the set of low-quality/questionable sources in two ways. First, we aggregate information using a list curated by NewsGuard [42]. NewsGuard is a journalistic organization that generally rates websites on their tendency to spread true or false information.
rob.item10_quote: Finally, low-quality/fake news sources (LQMS) account for 0.83% of original tweets and 0.19% of retweets.
